input_signals.name: Externally_Financed_Tangible_Buildout
input_signals.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(ADD(DELTA(dltt, 1), COALESCE(sstk, 0)), at)), RANK(NEG(RATIO(ADD(COALESCE(xrd, 0), COALESCE(intan, 0)), at))))
input_signals.hypothesis: Raising external debt and equity to fund expansion is most value-destructive at intangible-poor firms, which lack the knowledge assets needed to earn a spread over the cost of the new capital.
input_signals.reasoning: The external-financing anomaly and the intangible-intensity premium point in opposite directions, so their interaction should sharpen both: capital raised by intangible-lean, commodity-like producers is the clearest case of overinvestment. Conditioning the financing measure on low intangible intensity makes the mechanism about who is raising the money, not merely how much.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( rank( ratio( add( delta( dltt, 1 ), coalesce( sstk, 0 ) ), at ) ), rank( neg( ratio( add( coalesce( xrd, 0 ), coalesce( intan, 0 ) ), at ) ) ) )

input_signals.name: Growth_With_Weak_Intangible_Productivity
input_signals.hypothesis: Asset growth predicts low returns mainly when the existing capital base, measured inclusive of recognized intangibles, is already generating little revenue per dollar deployed; growth by capital-efficient firms is a positive-NPV signal instead.
input_signals.reasoning: Sales per unit of combined tangible and intangible capital is a direct measure of whether prior investment has been converted into output, so it identifies which growers are compounding an unproductive asset base. The interaction conditions the classic investment effect on intangible-inclusive capital productivity rather than treating all growth identically.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( rank( growth( at, 1 ) ), rank( neg( ratio( revt, add( coalesce( intan, 0 ), ppent ) ) ) ) )

input_signals.name: Knowledge_Pivot_Capex_Retrenchment
input_signals.hypothesis: A cut in the physical investment rate carries very different information depending on where the firm's productive capacity resides: for R&D-intensive firms it signals a deliberate pivot toward knowledge production (asset-light, high expected returns on expensed intangible capital), whereas for tangible-capital firms it is closer to ordinary capacity contraction.
input_signals.reasoning: The expression is multiplicative rather than additive, so it only lights up when a high R&D-to-assets firm simultaneously reduces its capex-to-PP&E rate, which is exactly the conditional claim rather than a sum of the R&D premium and the investment-decline effect. Scaling capex by the installed PP&E base and taking its first difference removes the mechanical "ratio rises because capex fell" artifact of the earlier mix variable, and using reported xrd (no zero-fill) prevents a large point mass at zero from destroying cross-sectional discrimination, at the cost of restricting the sample to firms for which the knowledge-pivot mechanism is even defined.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( rank( ratio( xrd, at ) ), rank( neg( delta( ratio( capx, ppent ), 1 ) ) ) )

input_signals.name: Plant_Buildout_Without_Knowledge_Capital
input_signals.hypothesis: The return penalty on gross plant expansion is concentrated among firms with essentially no accumulated knowledge capital, because capacity added without proprietary technology competes away its own rents; the same expansion by research-rich firms complements existing intangible capital and is not penalized.
input_signals.reasoning: Replacing the rank difference with a rank product makes the signal extreme only in the joint corner (fast PP&E growth AND a thin five-year R&D stock), which is the interaction the hypothesis asserts and which cannot be produced by stacking the PP&E-growth and R&D-intensity anomalies. Cumulating R&D over five years and scaling by sales measures the depth of the knowledge moat rather than one year of spending, and zero-filling is economically appropriate here because genuinely non-innovating firms are the intended conditioning group.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( rank( growth( ppegt, 1 ) ), rank( neg( ratio( ts_sum( coalesce( xrd, 0 ), 5 ), sale ) ) ) )

input_signals.name: Capacity_Expansion_Into_Eroding_Rents
input_signals.hypothesis: Gross margin is the realized cash return on a firm's intangible assets — brand, technology, and customer franchise — so a multi-year margin slide means those rents are eroding; firms that expand physical capacity into an eroding franchise are adding capacity to a commoditizing business and earn low subsequent returns.
input_signals.reasoning: This replaces the industry-neutralization robustness exercise with a different economic channel: the conditioner is the *realized output* of intangible capital rather than another measure of intangible input spending, so it is not a restatement of the archive's R&D-intensity leg. Because sale and cogs are near-universally reported, the conditioner has no zero mass point and full coverage, and its trend form captures franchise decay rather than a single noisy year.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( rank( growth( ppegt, 1 ) ), rank( neg( trend( ratio( sub( sale, cogs ), sale ), 3 ) ) ) )

input_signals.name: Acquired_Intangible_Heavy_Base_Low_Gross_Profitability
input_signals.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(ADD(COALESCE(gdwl, 0), COALESCE(intan, 0)), ADD(ppent, ADD(COALESCE(gdwl, 0), COALESCE(intan, 0))))), RANK(NEG(RATIO(SUB(sale, cogs), at))))
input_signals.hypothesis: A capital base dominated by purchased intangibles and goodwill rather than productive plant is only justified if those intangibles generate gross profit; when gross profitability is low, the carrying value is impairment-prone and the firm's past acquisition-driven investment was value-destroying, predicting low returns.
input_signals.reasoning: The previous share collapsed to 1.0 for every non-R&D reporter, but this composition measure uses balance-sheet stocks whose denominator always contains PP&E, so it is continuous and defined across the whole sample rather than acting as a reporting dummy. The mechanism is also different from the archive's financing and acquisition-flow signals: it asks whether the *accumulated* mix of purchased intangible versus physical capital is being validated by gross profit, making impairment risk, not current investment intensity, the source of predictability.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( rank( ratio( add( coalesce( gdwl, 0 ), coalesce( intan, 0 ) ), add( ppent, add( coalesce( gdwl, 0 ), coalesce( intan, 0 ) ) ) ) ), rank( neg( ratio( sub( sale, cogs ), at ) ) ) )

input_signals.name: Inventory_Buildup_Without_Pricing_Power
input_signals.hypothesis: Inventory accumulation is an investment decision whose payoff depends on brand and product differentiation: a commodity producer with no gross-margin cushion that builds stock is producing goods it will have to discount, whereas a high-margin, brand-supported firm can carry inventory profitably.
input_signals.reasoning: This opens the working-capital investment margin, which is untouched by the archive and largely orthogonal to CMA's asset-growth construction, while retaining the level gross-margin conditioner that has been the archive's most reliable intangible leg. Coverage is essentially full because inventory, sales, and cost of goods are near-universally reported, avoiding the zero-mass problem that has broken the FMB slopes of the R&D-conditioned signals.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( rank( ratio( delta( invt, 1 ), lag( at, 1 ) ) ), rank( neg( ratio( sub( sale, cogs ), sale ) ) ) )

input_signals.name: Young_Plant_Vintage_Without_Margin_Support
input_signals.hypothesis: A high net-to-gross PP&E ratio means the physical asset base is young — the firm has recently completed a heavy capital cycle — and when that fresh capacity sits in a business with no gross-margin cushion, the investment was made into a commoditizing market and will not earn its cost of capital.
input_signals.reasoning: Asset vintage is a stock measure of *cumulative recent* investment that is untouched by the archive and is much less collinear with the CMA factor's one-year asset-growth definition, so any alpha is less likely to be spanned by FF5. It is also naturally bounded between zero and one, avoiding the tail concentration that has decoupled FMB slopes from portfolio alphas in the flow-based signals.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( rank( ratio( ppent, ppegt ) ), rank( neg( ratio( sub( sale, cogs ), sale ) ) ) )

input_signals.name: Labor_Bloat_Relative_To_Output_Low_Margin
input_signals.hypothesis: Headcount growing faster than revenue is labor over-investment: the firm is adding fixed human cost without commensurate output, and at low-gross-profit firms there is no intangible margin to absorb the mistake, so returns are low.
input_signals.reasoning: The archive's two hiring signals both delivered alphas near −3.5% with FMB t-stats of only −1.7 to −1.8, consistent with raw employment growth being size- and cycle-driven rather than firm-specific over-hiring; differencing against contemporaneous sales growth removes the common cyclical component and should convert portfolio evidence into cross-sectional evidence. The conditioner is unchanged so the comparison isolates the design choice in the investment leg.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( rank( sub( growth( emp, 1 ), growth( sale, 1 ) ) ), rank( neg( ratio( sub( sale, cogs ), at ) ) ) )

input_signals.name: Capex_Rate_Without_Peer_Relative_Pricing_Power
input_signals.hypothesis: Physical investment is penalized when a firm has no differentiation advantage *relative to its own industry peers*: a below-peer gross margin means the firm holds no brand, technology, or process rent, so adding capacity into a market where competitors are more efficient destroys value.
input_signals.reasoning: The critic's spanning concern is that capex-to-assets times raw gross profitability reproduces CMA×RMW; industry-demeaning the margin removes the industry-level profitability structure that RMW sorts on and turns the conditioner into a firm-specific measure of intangible competitive position, while capex scaled by installed PP&E is an investment *rate* rather than the asset-growth definition CMA uses. Both changes push the construct away from the evaluating factor model while keeping the economics intact.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( rank( ratio( capx, ppent ) ), rank( neg( ind_adj( ratio( sub( sale, cogs ), sale ) ) ) ) )

input_signals.name: Cash_Burned_To_Purchase_Intangible_Assets
input_signals.hypothesis: Converting liquid, verifiable cash into illiquid, unverifiable intangible assets is the sharpest form of managerial empire building: the firm exchanges an asset investors can value at par for one whose worth depends entirely on management's own projections, and such conversions are followed by low returns.
input_signals.reasoning: This abandons the flow-restatement of the archive's best performer and opens the cash channel, which no evaluated signal has touched, so it cannot be a repackaging of the intangible-composition-times-gross-profitability result. The two legs are sourced from opposite sides of the balance sheet with no mechanical double counting — a firm can add intangibles without depleting cash (equity- or debt-financed) and it is precisely the cash-funded subset the hypothesis targets.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( rank( neg( delta( ratio( che, at ), 1 ) ) ), rank( ratio( delta( coalesce( intan, 0 ), 1 ), sale ) ) )

input_signals.name: Capacity_Overhang_Relative_To_Revenue_Base
input_signals.hypothesis: Physical capacity that has grown faster than the revenue it serves over a three-year horizon is an overhang: the firm has built plant it cannot fill, and at low-margin firms there is no pricing power to absorb the resulting under-utilization.
input_signals.reasoning: `Three_Year_Capex_Program_With_No_Revenue_Response` delivered a −3.3% alpha but a flat +0.20 FMB slope because both legs were asset-scaled dollar quantities with heavy skew; expressing the same economics as a difference of two three-year growth rates is exactly the transformation that converted the hiring-signal family from fmb −1.7 to −2.1 with a better Sharpe. The long horizon also separates this from the one-year investment measures that CMA spans.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( rank( sub( growth( ppegt, 3 ), growth( revt, 3 ) ) ), rank( neg( ratio( sub( sale, cogs ), at ) ) ) )

input_signals.name: Capital_Base_At_Peak_Versus_Revenue_Drawdown
input_signals.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(ADD(COALESCE(intan, 0), ppent), TS_MAX(ADD(COALESCE(intan, 0), ppent), 5))), RANK(NEG(RATIO(revt, TS_MAX(revt, 5)))))
input_signals.hypothesis: A firm whose combined physical and purchased-intangible capital sits at its own five-year maximum while revenue has fallen well below its own five-year peak is carrying an unwritten-down overhang; management has not yet retired capacity or impaired soft assets that the business no longer supports.
input_signals.reasoning: This abandons the flagship's composition-times-profitability structure entirely and uses a drawdown state — each quantity measured against its own history rather than against the cross-section — which is a different economic object (delayed capacity retirement and delayed impairment) and is not an investment-rate or profitability sort that CMA or RMW can span. Both legs are bounded in [0,1] by construction, which should give a stable cross-sectional ranking rather than the tail-driven spreads that produced flat FMB slopes earlier.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( rank( ratio( add( coalesce( intan, 0 ), ppent ), ts_max( add( coalesce( intan, 0 ), ppent ), 5 ) ) ), rank( neg( ratio( revt, ts_max( revt, 5 ) ) ) ) )

input_signals.name: Operating_Commitments_With_Below_Peer_Margin
input_signals.expression: MUL(SUMRANK(RATIO(DELTA(invt, 1), LAG(at, 1)), SUB(GROWTH(emp, 1), GROWTH(sale, 1))), RANK(NEG(IND_ADJ(RATIO(SUB(sale, cogs), sale)))))
input_signals.hypothesis: Inventory and headcount are the operating commitments managers add when they expect demand that does not arrive; making both while carrying a below-peer gross margin identifies firms over-extending in a market where competitors are better positioned.
input_signals.reasoning: The weighting objection is resolved by pooling exactly two channels, so each receives one half, and capex is deliberately dropped so the commitment leg contains only working-capital and labor margins that the CMA asset-growth factor does not measure. Industry-demeaning the margin conditioner removes the sector-level profitability structure RMW sorts on, making the surviving variation firm-specific competitive position rather than a repackaged profitability factor.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( sumrank( ratio( delta( invt, 1 ), lag( at, 1 ) ), sub( growth( emp, 1 ), growth( sale, 1 ) ) ), rank( neg( ind_adj( ratio( sub( sale, cogs ), sale ) ) ) ) )

input_signals.name: Liquidity_Drain_Without_Margin_Cushion
input_signals.hypothesis: Depleting the cash buffer is sustainable for a high-margin firm reinvesting from strength but is a warning sign at a low-margin firm, where the drain reflects operations consuming liquidity rather than opportunities being funded.
input_signals.reasoning: This repairs a specific archive failure: `Cash_Burned_To_Purchase_Intangible_Assets` had a strong cross-sectional slope (fmb −3.66) but zero portfolio alpha because its second leg (intangible purchases scaled by sales) was sparse and lumpy, fragmenting the extreme portfolios. Pairing the same liquidity channel with the conditioner that has repeatedly produced tradable spreads tests whether the cross-sectional signal can be converted into portfolio evidence, while keeping the mechanism (liquidity, not capital composition) distinct from the flagship family.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( rank( neg( delta( ratio( che, at ), 1 ) ) ), rank( neg( ratio( sub( sale, cogs ), at ) ) ) )

input_signals.name: Soft_Capital_Runoff_With_High_Capital_Turnover
input_signals.hypothesis: Firms that let their purchased intangible base run off — amortizing without replacing it through new acquisitions — while turning their remaining capital rapidly into revenue are running an efficient, self-funding operation whose lack of headline growth causes it to be overlooked.
input_signals.reasoning: The prior long-side attempt was a low-investment, high-gross-profitability position that CMA and RMW mechanically absorb; this version replaces physical disinvestment with *intangible* balance-sheet run-off and replaces margin with capital turnover, neither of which is an FF5 factor construction. It targets the archive's persistent weakness — every reliable result so far is short-side driven with modest Sharpe — by testing whether an economically distinct long state carries abnormal return.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( rank( neg( ratio( delta( coalesce( intan, 0 ), 1 ), lag( at, 1 ) ) ) ), rank( ratio( revt, add( coalesce( intan, 0 ), ppent ) ) ) )

input_signals.name: Soft_Capital_Runoff_With_Cash_Accumulation
input_signals.hypothesis: Genuine harvesting shows up as soft capital running off the balance sheet while cash builds: the firm is converting acquired intangibles into realized cash rather than replacing them with new purchases, and this self-funding discipline is underpriced.
input_signals.reasoning: This extends the archive's best Sharpe result by replacing its capital-turnover conditioner with the mirror image of the validated liquidity channel, so the two legs now describe the same managerial decision from the asset and the cash side — a stronger economic claim than run-off plus a static efficiency ratio. It also tests whether the liquidity axis is symmetric: the drain predicts poorly on the short side, so accumulation paired with soft-capital discipline should predict well on the long side.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( rank( neg( ratio( delta( coalesce( intan, 0 ), 1 ), sale ) ) ), rank( delta( ratio( che, at ), 1 ) ) )

input_signals.name: Working_Capital_Discipline_With_High_Capital_Turnover
input_signals.hypothesis: Firms shrinking inventory relative to their own sales growth while already generating high revenue per dollar of total capital are tightening an efficient operation; the absence of headline growth causes the market to overlook the improving cash conversion.
input_signals.reasoning: The long side has now been shown to work through capital turnover, but only via the intangible run-off margin; testing the working-capital margin under the same conditioner establishes whether the positive-side effect is a general capital-discipline phenomenon or specific to soft-asset amortization. The growth-differential form is the construction that repaired the FMB slope in the labor family, so it should deliver cross-sectional as well as portfolio evidence.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( rank( neg( sub( growth( invt, 1 ), growth( sale, 1 ) ) ) ), rank( ratio( revt, add( coalesce( intan, 0 ), ppent ) ) ) )

input_signals.name: Soft_Investment_Drift_Versus_Installed_Mix
input_signals.expression: MUL(RANK(SUB(RATIO(ADD(COALESCE(aqc, 0), DELTA(COALESCE(intan, 0), 1)), ADD(capx, ADD(COALESCE(aqc, 0), DELTA(COALESCE(intan, 0), 1)))), RATIO(COALESCE(intan, 0), ADD(ppent, COALESCE(intan, 0))))), RANK(NEG(RATIO(revt, ADD(COALESCE(intan, 0), ppent)))))
input_signals.hypothesis: When the marginal investment dollar is far softer than the installed asset base, the firm is drifting away from the business it knows — buying intangibles and companies rather than reinvesting in its own operations — and that drift destroys value most at firms whose existing capital already generates little revenue.
input_signals.reasoning: The construct compares the *composition of the flow* to the *composition of the stock*, a within-firm benchmark that no archive signal has used and that is scale-free and centered at zero by design, so it measures strategic drift rather than the level of investment or intangibility. Pairing it with the capital-turnover conditioner that has powered the archive's best results on both sides tests whether drift is punished specifically where the core business is already unproductive.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( rank( sub( ratio( add( coalesce( aqc, 0 ), delta( coalesce( intan, 0 ), 1 ) ), add( capx, add( coalesce( aqc, 0 ), delta( coalesce( intan, 0 ), 1 ) ) ) ), ratio( coalesce( intan, 0 ), add( ppent, coalesce( intan, 0 ) ) ) ) ), rank( neg( ratio( revt, add( coalesce( intan, 0 ), ppent ) ) ) ) )

input_signals.name: Capacity_Added_Without_Staffing_Low_Margin
input_signals.expression: MUL(RANK(MIN(GROWTH(ppegt, 1), SUB(GROWTH(ppegt, 1), GROWTH(emp, 1)))), RANK(NEG(RATIO(SUB(sale, cogs), at))))
input_signals.hypothesis: A firm that expands gross plant faster than it expands its workforce is building capacity it has not staffed to operate; at low-margin firms this unstaffed capacity is a fixed-cost commitment made without the rents to support it.
input_signals.reasoning: The MIN operator repairs the exact defect the critic identified — the score can only be high when plant growth is itself high *and* exceeds employment growth, so pure downsizing firms (falling headcount, flat plant) can no longer reach the top of the ranking. This makes the leg an unambiguous over-building measure rather than a restructuring proxy, and it is distinct from the archive's employment-minus-sales-growth leg because the benchmark is physical capacity rather than output.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( rank( min( growth( ppegt, 1 ), sub( growth( ppegt, 1 ), growth( emp, 1 ) ) ) ), rank( neg( ratio( sub( sale, cogs ), at ) ) ) )

input_signals.name: Soft_Capital_Being_Validated_In_Real_Time
input_signals.expression: MUL(RANK(SUB(GROWTH(revt, 1), GROWTH(ADD(COALESCE(intan, 0), ppent), 1))), RANK(RATIO(COALESCE(intan, 0), ADD(ppent, COALESCE(intan, 0)))))
input_signals.hypothesis: The flagship result says soft capital that fails to produce output is overpriced; the symmetric and untested claim is that soft capital which is *demonstrably* producing more output per year — revenue growing faster than the capital base — is underpriced, because investors discount intangible-heavy balance sheets indiscriminately.
input_signals.reasoning: This replaces the mechanical merger of two evaluated long-side signals with a new economic claim: it is the *improvement* in capital productivity, not its level, that identifies which intangible-heavy firms deserve their carrying values, and the conditioning direction (high soft-asset share) is the opposite of every prior negative signal, so the result is not predictable from the parents. Both legs are near-universally reported and the growth differential is scale-free, giving stable cross-sectional ranking.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( rank( sub( growth( revt, 1 ), growth( add( coalesce( intan, 0 ), ppent ), 1 ) ) ), rank( ratio( coalesce( intan, 0 ), add( ppent, coalesce( intan, 0 ) ) ) ) )

input_signals.name: Soft_Capital_Base_Without_Cash_Gross_Profit
input_signals.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(COALESCE(intan, 0), ADD(ppent, COALESCE(intan, 0)))), RANK(NEG(RATIO(SUB(SUB(sale, cogs), DELTA(invt, 1)), at))))
input_signals.hypothesis: Purchased intangible capital is validated only by profit that converts to cash; a soft-asset-heavy firm whose gross profit is being consumed by inventory accumulation has accounting profitability without cash generation, and the carrying value of its intangibles is correspondingly less defensible.
input_signals.reasoning: This asks a substantive economic question about the archive's flagship — does its power run through profitability per se, or through profitability that actually converts into cash — by deducting the inventory investment that absorbs gross profit, which also brings an investment-theme variable inside the conditioner rather than leaving it purely an accounting margin. If the cash-adjusted version strengthens the result it identifies the conversion channel; if it does not, the flagship is a pure margin effect and the final generation should stop refining it.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( rank( ratio( coalesce( intan, 0 ), add( ppent, coalesce( intan, 0 ) ) ) ), rank( neg( ratio( sub( sub( sale, cogs ), delta( invt, 1 ) ), at ) ) ) )

input_signals.name: Fully_Depreciated_Plant_Still_Earning_Rents
input_signals.expression: MUL(RANK(NEG(RATIO(ppent, ppegt))), RANK(RATIO(SUB(sale, cogs), ADD(ppent, COALESCE(intan, 0)))))
input_signals.hypothesis: A firm operating largely written-down plant that still generates high gross profit per dollar of remaining book capital holds productive capacity whose economic value far exceeds its carrying value; because book-based valuation understates these assets, such firms are systematically underpriced.
input_signals.reasoning: This drops the issuance leg the critic identified as a published anomaly and replaces it with asset vintage — a construct the archive has used only on the short side — while switching the validating measure from revenue turnover to gross profit per unit of capital, so neither component repeats a previously mined pairing. The economics are also specific rather than generic: old assets earning rents means the depreciation schedule, not the business, is what makes the firm look capital-light.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( rank( neg( ratio( ppent, ppegt ) ) ), rank( ratio( sub( sale, cogs ), add( ppent, coalesce( intan, 0 ) ) ) ) )

input_signals.name: Acquiring_When_Own_Labor_Productivity_Is_Depressed
input_signals.hypothesis: Managers buy revenue when their own organization has stopped producing it: purchasing companies and intangibles while output per employee sits at the bottom of its five-year range is a defensive deal made from operational weakness, and such deals disappoint.
input_signals.reasoning: The accounting linkage is broken because the conditioner no longer contains the capital base that acquisitions mechanically inflate — acquisitions add sales and employees roughly in proportion, so they do not push revenue per worker toward a trough by construction. Benchmarking labor productivity within the firm's own history also removes the industry determination that makes raw sales-per-employee unusable, and the timing framing (state *before* the deal) distinguishes this from the archive's post-acquisition disappointment signals.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( rank( ratio( add( coalesce( aqc, 0 ), delta( coalesce( intan, 0 ), 1 ) ), lag( at, 1 ) ) ), rank( neg( ts_rank( ratio( sale, emp ), 5 ) ) ) )

input_signals.name: Unverifiable_Young_Capital_Without_Cash_Profit
input_signals.expression: MUL(SUMRANK(RATIO(COALESCE(intan, 0), ADD(ppent, COALESCE(intan, 0))), RATIO(ppent, ppegt)), RANK(NEG(RATIO(SUB(SUB(sale, cogs), DELTA(invt, 1)), at))))
input_signals.hypothesis: Capital is least trustworthy when it is both soft (purchased intangibles rather than plant) and young (recently installed, not yet proven); when such a capital base fails to generate cash-converted gross profit, the carrying value rests entirely on management projections and returns are low.
input_signals.reasoning: The archive's two best-performing legs — intangible share of capital (short side) and plant vintage (long side, entering with the opposite sign) — are two measurements of the same latent quantity, the verifiability and provenness of the asset base, so combining them as an equal-weighted rank sum sharpens a single economic axis rather than averaging unrelated anomalies. Conditioning on cash gross profit rather than accounting margin follows the generation-7 finding that cash conversion is the stronger validator, and all inputs are near-universally reported.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( sumrank( ratio( coalesce( intan, 0 ), add( ppent, coalesce( intan, 0 ) ) ), ratio( ppent, ppegt ) ), rank( neg( ratio( sub( sub( sale, cogs ), delta( invt, 1 ) ), at ) ) ) )

input_signals.name: Soft_Investment_Drift_With_Floored_Denominator
input_signals.expression: MUL(RANK(SUB(RATIO(ADD(COALESCE(aqc, 0), DELTA(COALESCE(intan, 0), 1)), MAX(ADD(capx, ADD(COALESCE(aqc, 0), DELTA(COALESCE(intan, 0), 1))), capx)), RATIO(COALESCE(intan, 0), ADD(ppent, COALESCE(intan, 0))))), RANK(NEG(RATIO(revt, ADD(COALESCE(intan, 0), ppent)))))
input_signals.hypothesis: A firm whose marginal investment dollar is softer than its installed asset mix is drifting out of its core business, and that drift is punished where the existing capital already generates little revenue.
input_signals.reasoning: The parent drift signal worked on both metrics (fmb −3.07, alpha −2.2%, Sharpe −0.37) but its denominator could approach zero when intangibles amortize; my generation-7 replacement removed the instability by also dropping the installed-mix benchmark and lost the entire slope (−0.30), proving the benchmark carried the information. Flooring the denominator at capex preserves the benchmark while eliminating the sign flips — the minimal fix that separates measurement noise from economics.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( rank( sub( ratio( add( coalesce( aqc, 0 ), delta( coalesce( intan, 0 ), 1 ) ), max( add( capx, add( coalesce( aqc, 0 ), delta( coalesce( intan, 0 ), 1 ) ) ), capx ) ), ratio( coalesce( intan, 0 ), add( ppent, coalesce( intan, 0 ) ) ) ) ), rank( neg( ratio( revt, add( coalesce( intan, 0 ), ppent ) ) ) ) )

input_signals.name: Goodwill_Share_Of_Capital_Without_Cash_Profit

input_signals.hypothesis: Within the intangible base, goodwill is the component with no identifiable underlying asset and no contractual cash flows; if the soft-capital effect is really about unverifiability, restricting the numerator to goodwill while holding the full capital base in the denominator should concentrate the result.
input_signals.reasoning: This decomposes the archive's best signal along the one dimension that distinguishes purchased-but-identifiable intangibles (patents, customer lists, licences, which amortize on schedules tied to contracts) from pure acquisition premium, a question the archive has never been able to answer because earlier attempts changed the denominator at the same time. Holding the denominator fixed at total capital makes this a clean numerator decomposition whose outcome tells the final generation which component to build on.

input_signals.expression: MUL(RANK(NEG(RATIO(ppent, ppegt))), RANK(RATIO(SUB(SUB(sale, cogs), DELTA(invt, 1)), sale)))
input_signals.hypothesis: A firm operating heavily depreciated plant while earning a high cash-converted margin on every sales dollar is harvesting rents from capacity that its balance sheet no longer reflects; because book capital understates the productive asset, the market underprices the durable cash stream.
input_signals.reasoning: The mechanical dependence the critic identified is eliminated because the conditioner is now a margin scaled by sales, sharing no variable with the vintage leg, so the product tests the genuine interaction of asset age with pricing power rather than re-loading on low net PP&E twice. Retaining the cash adjustment keeps the generation-7 lesson that cash-converted profit is the more reliable validator, while the sales denominator makes the conditioner comparable across capital intensities.

input_signals.hypothesis: The terminal state for an intangible-heavy firm is one where the soft capital produces no cash profit and the cash buffer is simultaneously eroding: the write-down is coming and the firm will have to fund itself from weakness before it arrives.
input_signals.reasoning: The archive's two strongest and economically independent negative axes — soft-capital composition validated by cash profit (−4.9% alpha) and liquidity drain (−4.2% alpha, Sharpe −0.35) — have never been combined multiplicatively, and the generation-8 evidence shows that products sharpen while rank sums dilute, so the triple product should concentrate the short leg on firms failing on asset quality, profitability, and liquidity at once. All three components are near-universally reported, so coverage and portfolio stability should hold.

input_signals.name: Old_Plant_And_No_Purchased_Intangibles
input_signals.hypothesis: The archetypal underpriced firm on this axis operates written-down physical capacity and buys no soft capital: its assets are real, proven, and carried below economic value, and management is not spending shareholder money on unverifiable purchases.
input_signals.reasoning: Both legs are independently validated long-side constructs — plant vintage produced the archive's largest slope (+5.04) and intangible run-off produced its best Sharpe (+0.41) — and unlike the diluted rank-sum composite they are combined multiplicatively and share no variable, so the interaction identifies firms that are simultaneously asset-proven and acquisition-disciplined. This is the strongest available consolidation of the positive side, where the archive's evidence has been thinnest.
